 Haris Rauf urges Pakistan to target 350+, remains available for Test cricket 
 Pacer says domestic cricket is vital for improvement, dismisses criticism over sixes 
 Our Staff Reporter October 24, 2026 Newspaper , Sports Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Share on Facebook Share on Twitter LAHORE  - Pakistan fast bowler Haris Rauf has stressed the need for the national team to adapt to modern-day high-scoring cricket, saying posting totals of 350 or more and taking crucial wickets in the middle overs will be essential to succeeding in major International Cricket Council (ICC) events.
Speaking to the media in Lahore ahead of Pakistan’s next match in the ODI tri-series against England on Sunday, Rauf said teams could no longer rely on totals of around 300 as batting standards continued to rise across international cricket. “Nowadays, teams are scoring 350 and even 400 runs. We must adapt to these demands, put up bigger totals and find ways to defend them,” he said, highlighting the importance of improving both batting and bowling performances.
The pacer identified middle-over breakthroughs as a key component of Pakistan’s bowling strategy, noting that bowlers were under pressure to contain increasingly aggressive batters worldwide. He also pointed out that the ball change after 34 overs could influence bowling conditions and make it important for the attack to capitalise on opportunities.
He expressed satisfaction with Pakistan’s start to the tri-series, praising the team’s collective performance. While acknowledging that Fakhar Zaman and Saim Ayub had been unable to make significant contributions in the previous two matches, he backed the middle order for stepping up when required. “Cricket is a team game, and every player has a role to play,” he said.
Rauf also welcomed the reunion of Pakistan’s pace trio, comprising Shaheen Shah Afridi, Naseem Shah and himself. He said the bowlers were focused on taking wickets and supporting one another, adding that bowling alongside Shaheen was particularly enjoyable. “Pace remains an X-factor in modern cricket,” Rauf said, emphasising that he continued to work on his fitness and speed to strengthen his effectiveness.
Brushing aside criticism over conceding sixes, the fast bowler maintained that such setbacks were part of the game. “It is not just me who gets hit for sixes; every bowler in the world goes through it,” he said, adding that he had never insisted on bowling exclusively at the start or end of an innings and always followed the team’s requirements. Rauf also underlined the importance of domestic cricket in improving players’ skills, saying cricketers should participate whenever their schedules allow. He confirmed that he remained available for Test cricket and believed domestic competition was essential for development and match readiness. The pacer praised bowling coach Shaun Tait, who has previously worked with Pakistan, expressing confidence in the coaching staff and its understanding of the players. Meanwhile, Rauf urged fans to support the October 25 match dedicated to breast cancer awareness, saying sporting events provide an important platform to promote meaningful causes.
